meta.note: R15.2 quiz contract: items[].{id,nodeId,prompt,options[{text,explain}],correct,sourceRef?,source_ref?}. sourceRef is the in-page anchor; source_ref is the paper section, validated and surfaced as sectionRef. Authored from page content only — never invent values the page doesn't support.

items.prompt: SHD and SID both score an estimated DAG against the true one. What does SID count that SHD does not?

options.text: Ordered node pairs whose intervention distribution the estimate gets wrong
options.explain: Yes — SID counts the pairs for which the estimated graph fails to give a correct interventional prediction, which is why it can disagree sharply with edge counting.

options.text: Edges present in one graph but absent in the other
options.explain: No — that is SHD. It counts edge-level disagreement and says nothing about causal inference capacity.

options.text: The number of v-structures the two graphs disagree on
options.explain: No — the paper does not define SID in terms of v-structure disagreement.

options.text: The total variation distance between the two observational distributions
options.explain: No — SID is a purely graphical criterion; it never estimates or compares distributions numerically.

items.prompt: Why is SID called a *pre-*distance rather than a metric?

options.text: It fails symmetry — swapping the true and estimated graph can change the value
options.explain: Correct. The paper's own example is a non-empty graph versus the empty DAG: the empty DAG makes every set a valid adjustment set, so one direction is trivially 'correct' and the other is not.

options.text: It can take negative values
options.explain: No — SID counts pairs, so it satisfies non-negativity.

options.text: It is undefined when the two graphs are identical
options.explain: No — the paper characterizes exactly when SID equals zero; identical graphs are a well-defined case.

options.text: It violates the triangle inequality for CPDAGs only
options.explain: No — the asymmetry is the stated reason, and it applies to DAGs, not just CPDAGs.

items.prompt: For the running graphs G: A→B, A→C, B→D, C→D and H=G+(B→C), which pairs are wrong when the arguments are swapped to SID(H,G)?

options.text: Exactly (C,B) and (C,D), so SID(H,G)=2
options.explain: Correct — estimate G omits true H-parent B from C's adjustment set, leaving the direct back-door route to B and the fork through B to D unblocked.

options.text: No pairs, because G and H have the same skeleton
options.explain: No — H has the extra B→C edge, and swapping the truth role turns its omission into two intervention errors.

options.text: All 12 ordered pairs
options.explain: No — only source C has a mismatched parent set in this direction, and only targets B and D fail.

items.prompt: What problem does the equivalent graphical formulation of SID solve?

options.text: The causal definition is hard to compute, so SID is restated as a valid-adjustment-set check
options.explain: Right — the reformulation turns a statement about interventional distributions into a structural question that can be checked by walking paths in the graph.

options.text: It removes SID's dependence on the true graph
options.explain: No — the reformulation still asks whether a set is a valid adjustment set *relative to the true DAG*.

options.text: It makes SID symmetric
options.explain: No — symmetry is addressed separately, by the symmetrization extension.

options.text: It extends SID from DAGs to CPDAGs
options.explain: No — the CPDAG extensions are a different section; this reformulation is about computability.

items.prompt: SID uses the parent set as the adjustment set by default. According to the paper, why that choice?

options.text: It is easy to compute and depends only on the neighbourhood of the intervened nodes
options.explain: Correct — and the authors are explicit that this is a design choice, not a necessity: any other adjustment-set method could be substituted.

options.text: It is the only set that is provably valid for every DAG
options.explain: No — minimal adjustment sets are named as a valid alternative, so the parent set is not unique in validity.

options.text: It always yields the smallest possible adjustment set
options.explain: No — minimal adjustment sets are described as the *smaller* alternative; the parent set is not minimal.

options.text: It makes the resulting distance symmetric
options.explain: No — the choice of adjustment set is unrelated to SID's asymmetry.

items.prompt: What situation motivates a symmetrized SID?

options.text: Two DAGs where neither can be regarded as an estimate of the other
options.explain: Yes — with no ground-truth graph, the directional definition has no principled orientation, so the two directions are combined.

options.text: Comparing a DAG against a CPDAG
options.explain: No — that case is handled by the DAG-versus-CPDAG extension, which produces a lower and upper bound instead.

options.text: When the true graph contains hidden variables
options.explain: No — hidden variables are explicitly listed as future work, not the motivation for symmetrization.

options.text: When SID and SHD disagree about which estimate is better
options.explain: No — the paper motivates symmetrization by the absence of a ground-truth graph, not by disagreement with SHD.

items.prompt: Over what class of graphs is SHD defined in this paper?

options.text: Partially directed acyclic graphs (PDAGs), of which DAGs are a special case
options.explain: Correct — that is why one definition covers DAG-vs-DAG, PDAG-vs-PDAG, and DAG-vs-PDAG comparisons alike.

options.text: Directed acyclic graphs only
options.explain: No — restricting to DAGs would not cover the PDAG comparisons the paper makes.

options.text: Arbitrary directed graphs, including cyclic ones
options.explain: No — acyclicity is part of the definition.

options.text: Undirected graphs only
options.explain: No — SHD compares edge *types*, which requires orientation information.

items.prompt: The paper reports roughly quadratic/cubic timing curves but gives a quartic dense worst-case bound. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: The observations describe sampled graph families; the quartic result is a worst-case ceiling, so both can be true
options.explain: Correct — empirical average behavior over finite graph families can remain below an asymptotic worst-case upper bound.

options.text: The timing experiment disproves the quartic worst-case bound
options.explain: No — a finite average-case experiment cannot disprove a worst-case upper bound.

options.text: Sparse and dense SID have exactly quadratic and cubic complexity for every input
options.explain: No — those are approximate observed trends, not universal complexity guarantees.

items.prompt: Why does SID against an estimated CPDAG return lower and upper bounds instead of one score?

options.text: Different DAGs in the represented equivalence class can imply different SID values
options.explain: Correct — the bounds summarize the best and worst compatible DAG extensions.

options.text: The observational sample size is unknown
options.explain: No — the bounds arise from orientation ambiguity in the equivalence class, not sampling uncertainty.

options.text: SHD must be averaged with SID
options.explain: No — SHD is a separate comparison measure and is not part of these bounds.

items.prompt: The running estimate $H$ holds every edge of the true graph $G$ plus the extra edge $B\to C$. Why does the page call $H$'s parent sets safe for $G$?

options.text: Each is a superset of $G$'s parent set, and adjusting for extra ancestors does not break the calculation
options.explain: Yes. $G\subseteq H$ makes every $H$ parent set a superset adjustment set, which is exactly the containment the zero-SID proof needs.

options.text: The two graphs have the same skeleton
options.explain: No. $H$ carries an edge $G$ does not, so the skeletons differ by that pair.

options.text: An SHD of one is below the threshold at which adjustment stops being valid
options.explain: No. There is no such threshold; SHD does not bound adjustment validity at all, which is the whole reason SID exists.

options.text: The extra edge is undirected, so it contributes no parent
options.explain: No. $B\to C$ is directed, and it is precisely what adds $B$ to $C$'s parent set in $H$.

items.prompt: SID fixes one prediction procedure — parent adjustment. What does fixing it buy?

options.text: It makes SID computable from graph structure alone, given Markovianity to the true DAG
options.explain: Correct. Without a fixed procedure the comparison would depend on which adjustment set a reader happened to pick.

options.text: It guarantees the smallest adjustment set for every pair
options.explain: No. Minimal sets are a separate design choice the paper studies on its own; parents are often not minimal.

options.text: It makes SID symmetric in its two arguments
options.explain: No. SID stays asymmetric — swapping truth and estimate can change the count.

options.text: It removes the need to know the true graph
options.explain: No. Correctness is still defined against the true graph's intervention distributions.

items.prompt: Two estimates each sit at SHD one: one adds an edge, one reverses an edge. Predict which damages intervention predictions.

options.text: The reversal, because the intervened node loses the parent it needed to block confounding
options.explain: Right. The paper reports eight erroneous predictions for the reversal, while the added edge costs nothing.

options.text: The added edge, because it introduces an extra parameter to estimate
options.explain: No. The extra adjustment variable is conditionally irrelevant given the true parents, so every pair stays correct.

options.text: Both, equally — one edge of damage each
options.explain: No. That is exactly SHD's verdict, and the divergence from it is what motivates SID.

options.text: Neither, since SHD one is a single local change
options.explain: No. A local edit can have global consequences; that asymmetry is the point of the example.

items.prompt: Compare $A\to B\to C$ with $A\to B\leftarrow C$. What does conditioning on $B$ do?

options.text: Closes the chain and opens the collider
options.explain: Correct, and it is why the same three nodes encode opposite path-blocking behaviour.

options.text: Closes both paths
options.explain: No. A collider is closed by default and conditioning on it opens the path.

options.text: Opens both paths
options.explain: No. A chain closes when you condition on its middle node.

options.text: Opens the chain and closes the collider
options.explain: No — this is the two cases the wrong way round.

items.prompt: An edge in a CPDAG is left undirected. What does that record?

options.text: Members of the Markov equivalence class disagree about its orientation
options.explain: Yes. A CPDAG directs an edge only where every member of the class agrees.

options.text: The edge is confounded by an unobserved common cause
options.explain: No. That is what a bidirected edge marks in an ADMG, a different object.

options.text: The orientation is unknown because of missing data
options.explain: No. The ambiguity is structural: observational data cannot distinguish Markov-equivalent DAGs however much of it you have.

options.text: The edge may be deleted without changing the class
options.explain: No. The edge is present in every member; only its direction varies.

items.prompt: When do conditioning on $X=x$ and setting $X$ to $x$ give the same answer for $Y$?

options.text: When $X$ has no confounded relationship with $Y$
options.explain: Correct. Confounding is exactly what makes the observed association differ from the effect of acting.

options.text: Whenever the graph is acyclic
options.explain: No. Acyclicity is assumed throughout and does not remove confounding.

options.text: Whenever the distribution is Gaussian
options.explain: No. The gap is structural, not distributional; a linear Gaussian SEM can be badly confounded.

options.text: Whenever $X$ and $Y$ are marginally independent
options.explain: No. Marginal independence can coexist with a real effect that a second path cancels.

items.prompt: In a linear Gaussian SEM you intervene on $X$. What happens to $Y$'s variance?

options.text: It is unchanged — the intervention replaces only $X$'s own noise source
options.explain: Right. The intervention shifts downstream means proportionally while leaving every other mechanism, and so the variance, intact.

options.text: It collapses to zero, because $X$ is now fixed
options.explain: No. Fixing $X$ removes $X$'s noise, not the noise of every variable downstream of it.

options.text: It scales with the value $X$ is set to
options.explain: No. The model is linear with additive noise; the set value moves means, not spreads.

options.text: It becomes the covariance between $X$ and $Y$
options.explain: No. A variance and a covariance are different quantities, and the intervention does not equate them.

items.prompt: An estimate scores $\mathrm{SID}=0$ but carries strictly more edges than the truth. What does the paper propose?

options.text: Report a separate added-edge count beside SID, because SID scores effects and not parsimony
options.explain: Correct. The two numbers are orthogonal, and the edge count serves readers who value parsimony independently.

options.text: Treat SID zero as proof the graphs are identical
options.explain: No. Zero SID means every estimated adjustment set stays valid, which a strict superset can achieve.

options.text: Fall back to SHD, since SID has failed here
options.explain: No. SID has not failed; it answered the causal question correctly and a different question needs a different number.

options.text: Divide SID by the edge count to penalise density
options.explain: No. The paper keeps the measures separate rather than blending them into one score.

items.prompt: The estimate gives a source node exactly the same parents as the true graph. What may the algorithm do?

options.text: Skip that whole source — the true back-door set is valid for every target
options.explain: Correct, and it is a per-source skip, not a per-pair one, which is where the saving comes from.

options.text: Skip only the pairs whose target is a child of that source
options.explain: No. Matching parents make the set valid for every target, not a subset of them.

options.text: Skip the check only when the source has no parents at all
options.explain: No. The condition is that the parent sets agree, which an empty set satisfies but does not require.

options.text: Nothing — each ordered pair must still be checked separately
options.explain: No. Checking every pair regardless is the naive shape the implementation exists to avoid.

items.prompt: Why do both algorithms fix a source and answer for every target at once?

options.text: Reachability computed once for a source serves all its targets, turning each target's verdict into a lookup
options.explain: Right. Sharing the expensive closure across all $p-1$ targets is what keeps SID computable on graphs of a few hundred nodes.

options.text: Because d-separation is undefined for a single ordered pair
options.explain: No. It is perfectly well defined per pair; calling it per pair is simply wasteful.

options.text: Because the adjustment set changes with every target
options.explain: No. The adjustment set is the source's estimated parent set and is fixed once the source is.

options.text: Because the true graph must be rebuilt for each source anyway
options.explain: No. The graph is fixed; only the conditioned-tail copy is derived, and that too is per source.

items.prompt: The implementation builds two matrix routines. What do they correspond to?

options.text: The two halves of the adjustment criterion: a directed-reachability closure, and a search for open non-causal routes
options.explain: Correct. One asks whether a causal path exists and where the parent set sits on it; the other finds every node reachable by an open, non-causal path.

options.text: One for the true graph and one for the estimated graph
options.explain: No. Both routines are computed against the true graph; the estimate supplies the adjustment set.

options.text: One for DAGs and one for CPDAGs
options.explain: No. The CPDAG case is handled by which graphs are compared, not by a separate matrix routine here.

options.text: One for the forward SID direction and one for the reverse
options.explain: No. Asymmetry comes from swapping the arguments and re-running, not from a second routine.

items.prompt: Why does the proof treat an omitted parent so much more harshly than an added one?

options.text: Extra ancestors are slack the adjustment can absorb; a missing parent leaves genuine confounding unblocked
options.explain: Correct. Extra edges elsewhere cannot repair the hole, which is why the containment hypothesis runs in one direction only.

options.text: Added edges are cheaper to detect, so they are penalised less
options.explain: No. The asymmetry is about the validity of the adjustment, not about detection cost.

options.text: Because an omitted parent always reverses an edge as well
options.explain: No. A parent can be omitted by deletion, with no reversal involved.

options.text: Because SID counts unordered pairs, which doubles omission errors
options.explain: No. SID counts ordered pairs, and that ordering is what makes it asymmetric.

items.prompt: A single SHD unit separates two graphs. How far can SID move, and why?

options.text: By a bounded amount, because one edge changes parent sets only at its two endpoints
options.explain: Correct, and the bound is sharp: an explicit one-edge flip attains it, so it is worst case rather than loose.

options.text: Not at all — one edge cannot change any intervention distribution
options.explain: No. That is the SHD-zero case; one edit can and does move SID.

options.text: Without bound, since a single edge sits on arbitrarily many paths
options.explain: No. Every node other than the edge's two endpoints keeps its adjustment logic untouched, which is what bounds the damage.

options.text: By exactly one, matching the SHD unit
options.explain: No. The two measures live on different scales; a single edit can spoil a whole treatment row.

items.prompt: SID is defined through the existence of a discriminating distribution, not as a literal count of wrong effects. What did the second experiment establish?

options.text: That the abstract definition and the practical count of wrongly estimated effects coincide almost perfectly
options.explain: Correct, and that is what lets practitioners read SID as a count when comparing causal-discovery methods.

options.text: That SID and SHD are strongly correlated after all
options.explain: No. The first experiment found them nearly uncorrelated, which is the point of introducing SID.

options.text: That SID is an upper bound on the number of wrong effects, never tight
options.explain: No. The experiment reports agreement, not a loose one-sided bound.

options.text: That the discriminating distribution can always be constructed by hand
options.explain: No. The experiment measures agreement of two quantities; it does not construct witnesses.

items.prompt: An unobserved $U$ causes both $X$ and $Y$, so $p(y\mid do(x))$ is not recoverable from any observed adjustment set. How should the pair be scored?

options.text: Excluded from the count — the pair is unanswerable, not answered wrongly
options.explain: Correct, and it mirrors how the CPDAG case excludes what cannot be judged rather than penalising it.

options.text: Counted as an SID error, since the estimate failed to predict it
options.explain: No. Scoring it as a mistake would punish a method for a limit of the data rather than a fault of the graph.

options.text: Counted as correct, since no estimate could do better
options.explain: No. Crediting it would inflate every method equally and hide the identifiability problem.

options.text: Scored by substituting the nearest identifiable pair
options.explain: No. The roadmap excludes non-identifiable effects; it does not substitute for them.
